smell: Script sets `set -eu` but omits `-o pipefail`, while executing pipelines on the critical download and verification paths (latest-version resolver, checksum extract, sha256sum). A broken upstream pipe stage silently succeeds if the last stage succeeds, masking corruption.
evidence:
set -eu
...
VERSION=$(curl -sSfL "https://api.github.com/..." |
    sed -n 's/.*"tag_name": *"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' |
    head -1)
...
EXPECTED=$(grep " $ARCHIVE_NAME\$" "$TMP/SHA256SUMS" | awk '{print $1}')
ACTUAL=$($SHA_CMD "$TMP/$ARCHIVE_NAME" | awk '{print $1}')
fix_summary: Replace `set -eu` with `set -euo pipefail`. Note that `/bin/sh` (dash) does not implement `pipefail`; either switch shebang to `#!/usr/bin/env bash` and add pipefail, or keep POSIX `sh` and add explicit exit-code checks after each piped command. Current emptiness guards (line 74, 123) catch some cases but not partial corruption.

smell: Shebang `#!/bin/sh` constrains the script to POSIX sh (dash on Debian/Ubuntu, ash on Alpine), which prevents adopting `set -o pipefail`, `[[ ]]`, and other conveniences that would harden this script. The skill prefers `#!/usr/bin/env bash` for portability+features.
fix_summary: Consider `#!/usr/bin/env bash` if you want pipefail + bashisms. Alternatively keep `/bin/sh` as an intentional portability choice (installers that run under busybox ash on Alpine Linux docker images) — but then document that choice in a one-line comment above the shebang so future contributors don't accidentally introduce bashisms.

smell: `tar -xzf` runs with no hardening flags (`--no-same-owner`, `--no-same-permissions`, no member filter) inside a temp dir. A malicious release tarball with `..` entries or absolute paths could escape $TMP. The archive is now both sha256-verified and cosign-signed, so the attack surface requires compromising the release signing pipeline — but `tar` hardening is cheap defense-in-depth.
evidence:
cd "$TMP"
tar -xzf "$ARCHIVE_NAME"

[ -f "$BINARY" ] || die "$BINARY not found in archive"
fix_summary: Add `--no-same-owner --no-same-permissions` to the tar invocation. Consider `tar -tzf` first to list members, grep-check for `^/` or `\.\./`, abort on match. GNU tar also supports `--restrict`. Goreleaser archives have a known-flat layout (binary + docs), so the check is cheap.

smell: Checksum extraction uses `grep " $ARCHIVE_NAME\$"` where `$ARCHIVE_NAME` ends with `.tar.gz`. In BRE, `.` matches any character, so the regex would also match artifact names like `okdctlX0X1X0XLinuxXx86_64XtarXgz`. The cosign signature guarantees SHA256SUMS integrity so exploitation requires release-pipeline compromise, but `grep -F` is the idiomatic fixed-string match and closes the residual ambiguity.
evidence:
EXPECTED=$(grep " $ARCHIVE_NAME\$" "$TMP/SHA256SUMS" | awk '{print $1}')
[ -n "$EXPECTED" ] || die "no checksum found for $ARCHIVE_NAME in SHA256SUMS"
fix_summary: Swap `grep " $ARCHIVE_NAME\$"` for `awk -v name="$ARCHIVE_NAME" '$2 == name {print $1}'` (exact field match on a single pass) or `grep -F -- " $ARCHIVE_NAME"` + an additional end-of-line check. Keeps the leading-space anchor (prevents partial-name prefix match) and adds exact-name matching.

smell: `cosign verify-blob ... >/dev/null 2>&1 || die` silences cosign's diagnostic output when verification fails. The user sees only `cosign signature verification failed on SHA256SUMS` with no clue whether the cert identity mismatched, the OIDC issuer changed, the file was tampered with, or cosign itself crashed. Debuggability on a security-critical path matters.
evidence:
COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL=1 cosign verify-blob \
    --certificate="$TMP/SHA256SUMS.pem" \
    --signature="$TMP/SHA256SUMS.sig" \
    --certificate-identity-regexp='...' \
    --certificate-oidc-issuer='https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com' \
    "$TMP/SHA256SUMS" >/dev/null 2>&1 ||
    die "cosign signature verification failed on SHA256SUMS"
fix_summary: Drop the `>/dev/null 2>&1` redirect; cosign's success output is quiet enough to tolerate on stderr, and its failure output names the exact cause (certificate identity mismatch vs signature mismatch vs missing file). Alternative: capture stderr to a temp file, print on failure only.
rule_source: Go proverb: clear is better than clever

smell: `required_version = ">= 1.2"` is an open-ended floor. Terraform 2.x (if/when HashiCorp ships it) or an OpenTofu divergence could break compatibility, and CI pins 1.10.3 while the module accepts anything >= 1.2 — a 4.5-year version gap.
fix_summary: Tighten to `required_version = ">= 1.10, < 2.0"` to match the CI matrix and prevent accidental adoption of a future major. Same treatment to `environments/production/versions.tf`.

smell: `efi_disk` blocks have no lifecycle guard. If a config change on bootstrap forces replacement (e.g. changing `os_storage`, `bios`, `machine`), Terraform will destroy the EFI disk before creating the new one — losing boot-order nvram state that persists kernel args and bootloader choices.
fix_summary: Consider adding `efi_disk` to the `ignore_changes` list for each VM resource so EFI nvram state is preserved across Terraform applies (matching the existing network_device/cdrom/boot_order pattern). Low confidence because EFI nvram loss on VM replace is often acceptable for a cluster where nodes are reprovisioned from ISO — but worth a roadmap note.

smell: Master VMs (the OKD control plane carrying etcd quorum state) have no `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` guard. A misconfigured `terraform apply` that perturbs a force-new attribute (e.g. `bios`, `machine`, `os_storage`) would silently destroy and replace every master, losing etcd state. `okdctl destroy` is the intended destruction path; `terraform apply` should not be able to accidentally tear down the control plane.
fix_summary: Add `prevent_destroy = true` to the master VM resource's `lifecycle` block, optionally gated by a variable (e.g. `var.allow_master_destroy`) that the `okdctl destroy` command flips to false before running Terraform. Documentation in main.tf should state that operators MUST use `okdctl destroy` to tear down a cluster. Mirrors the typical `prevent_destroy` pattern on quorum-sensitive resources (RDS instances, etcd volumes).

smell: Pre-commit hooks fmt+vet Go but run no `shellcheck` on scripts/install.sh despite it being the user-facing sudo-ran installer. CI also skips shellcheck — so `install.sh` lint failures land in main undetected until release.
evidence:
pre-commit:
  parallel: true
  commands:
    gofumpt:
      glob: "*.go"
      run: gofumpt -l -w {staged_files}
      stage_fixed: true
    govet:
      run: go vet ./...
fix_summary: Add a `shellcheck` command to lefthook.yml pre-commit, scoped to `*.sh`. Also add a shellcheck CI job to `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (lint-shell). ShellCheck catches SC2086 (unquoted expansion), SC2046 (word split), SC3040 (non-POSIX pipefail in /bin/sh) at build time — cheaper than finding them post-release when `install.sh` is sudo-ran on a stranger's laptop.

smell: `validate-terraform` job runs only `terraform fmt -check` + `terraform validate`. No tflint, tfsec, or checkov — the latter two catch secrets in locals, missing `sensitive`, provider pinning, and state-backend smells that would land here on future HCL contributions.
evidence:
validate-terraform:
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@...
    - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@...
      with:
        terraform_version: "1.10.3"
    - run: terraform fmt -check -recursive infrastructure/terraform
    - working-directory: ...
      run: terraform init -backend=false && terraform validate
fix_summary: Add two steps to the `validate-terraform` job: (1) `tflint --recursive` after a brief `tflint --init`; (2) `tfsec infrastructure/terraform` or `trivy config infrastructure/terraform`. Both have maintained GitHub Actions (terraform-linters/setup-tflint, aquasecurity/tfsec-action). The HCL surface is small today — lock it down now.
